sentences.text: The HathiTrust Digital Library, or HathiTrust, is a digital library: a large-scale collaborative repository of digital content from research libraries, administered by the University of Michigan, and catalogued among American digital libraries, full-text scholarly online databases and mass digitization.

Its collection is of books, journals and government documents digitized from libraries around the world and dated from 1500 to the present: content digitized through Google Books and the Internet Archive, beside collections that member libraries digitized themselves, aggregated in one shared repository; the census keeps it apart from Google Books on that ground and records the Internet Archive as a source it uses.

In September 2024 it comprised more than 18 million volumes, 6.7 million of them in the public domain in the United States; the University of Michigan Library gives the public domain as more than a third of the collection and the items preserved as more than 17 million, and the library's research guide quotes HathiTrust's own figure of 18+ million digitized items.
Its name is the Hindi word for elephant, from the Sanskrit hastin, an animal famed for its long-term memory, and it is a distinct entity from HATII.

HathiTrust was founded in October 2008 by the twelve universities of the Committee on Institutional Cooperation and the eleven libraries of the University of California, its infrastructure put in place at the University of Michigan, which has scanned and deposited more than 4.8 million items.

It is a nonprofit collaborative of academic and research libraries, owned as a university consortium with the University of Michigan as its parent: as of 2024 more than 219 research libraries across the United States, Canada and Europe, under a shared governance structure, with costs shared by the participating libraries and library consortia.
Its executive director is Mike Furlough, who succeeded the founding director John Wilkin after Wilkin stepped down in 2013.

Its Shared Print Program is a distributed collective collection whose participating libraries have committed to retaining almost 18 million monograph volumes for 25 years, three-quarters of its digital book holdings.

sentences.sense: access by copyright status and by place
sentences.text: What a reader may see follows copyright: items in the public domain, more than a third of the collection, are fully available for everyone, while many items are protected by copyright and cannot be viewed in full without the express permission of the copyright holder.

sentences.sense: access by copyright status and by place
sentences.text: Its copyright policy, as Wikipedia quotes it for 2021, says that protected works cannot ordinarily be displayed in large portions without permission and that access to a work is restricted until its copyright or permission status can be established; the census knows the policy only through that quotation and, on that restriction, counts the library outside the open full-text libraries for works in copyright.

sentences.sense: access by copyright status and by place
sentences.text: Access also turns on where the reader is, and the sources date the line differently: Wikipedia quotes the policy as restricting users outside the United States from works published outside the United States after and including 1896, and the University of Michigan's guide quotes HathiTrust's web site as estimating 1898 the earliest date at which foreign works may still be in copyright, so that works published abroad from 1898 through 1928 are open to United States IP addresses and closed to others.

sentences.sense: access by affiliation and the reader's tools
sentences.text: Access turns as well on affiliation: a member's community gains additional access by logging in, and at the University of Michigan logged-in users can download complete public-domain books, where guests download one page at a time.

sentences.sense: access by affiliation and the reader's tools
sentences.text: A volume, a digitized book or other publication, is viewed in PageTurner, the site's web application, in which a reader can navigate a publication, download a PDF of it and view its pages one at a time, scrolling, flipping or as thumbnails.

sentences.sense: access by affiliation and the reader's tools
sentences.text: Through the Emergency Temporary Access Service, users of member libraries can in special situations, such as a library's closure for a public health emergency, obtain lawful access to copyright digital materials in place of the physical books their library holds.

sentences.sense: access by affiliation and the reader's tools
sentences.text: Patrons with print disabilities can obtain downloaded copies of anything in the collection through its Accessible Text Request Service.

Its discovery services include full-text search across the entire repository: researchers search the catalogue's descriptive data, the contents of digitized items, or both, and works still under copyright carry a "Limited (search-only)" status within which a reader can still search for key terms.

The census reads the record as answering whether a volume is held, by full-text search, whether its pages may be shown or only searched, and the scale of the holdings, and it ran no search of its own.

In September 2011 the Authors Guild sued HathiTrust, alleging massive copyright violation, and in October 2012 a federal court found HathiTrust's use of books scanned by Google to be fair use under US law, its opinion resting on the transformativeness doctrine.

The Second Circuit largely affirmed the decision on 10 June 2014, finding that providing search and accessibility for the visually impaired were grounds to consider the service transformative and fair use, and remanded to the lower court whether the plaintiffs had standing over HathiTrust's library preservation copies.

The census reads Authors Guild v. HathiTrust, as Wikipedia reports it, as the record's precedent for a machine reading of whole books whose product is a finding, search, while the pages stay closed; in its record, what an apparatus makes from a work there is a full-text search index the courts held transformative and fair use.

Computational analysis of the volumes was the separate service of the HathiTrust Research Center, established in 2011 as a partnership of Indiana University, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and HathiTrust to enable computational analysis of the library, which supported scholars using text and data mining methods in educational and non-profit research; the census holds the Center as a part of the library and as a distinct entity.

In October 2024 HathiTrust's executive director announced that funding for the Center would cease at the end of 2026, when it will be formally closed; its services were discontinued on 30 September 2026, its accounts, algorithms and data capsules with them, some of its resources remain usable without an account, and access to the Digital Library remains open.

Its saved sources say nothing of training use and tie none of the library's volumes to model training, whether a work keeps its author's name there is not recorded, and the census does not record the library as a training corpus.
The census reads HathiTrust in three layers kept apart: holdings, access restricted where copyright status cannot be established, and computational availability, the Research Center's, now ended.

The archive's Originals Library has met HathiTrust as a holder of open witnesses its sessions could not reach: on 15 October 2026 a seating found HathiTrust not reachable from its workspace for Pound's public-domain first printings of the Cantos, a seating of 27 October 2026 queued Langston Hughes's Fine Clothes to the Jew (1927), whose one open scan is at HathiTrust, as unreachable, and on 30 October 2026 HathiTrust, holding Cornell's volumes 36–37 of the Monatshefte in full view, refused the seating's requests with a Cloudflare challenge and a block page.

Other witnesses the archive seated came by way of HathiTrust: its first edition of The Souls of Black Folk is the Northwestern University copy (HathiTrust ien.35556032538837) uploaded to the Internet Archive, and its Tribüne volume is the University of Michigan copy digitized by Google, held by reference via HathiTrust and the Internet Archive, which HathiTrust records as pdus, public domain in the United States, full view.
The archive's bibliography places its author's doctoral dissertation, Strange New Canons (University of Michigan, 2013), at a HathiTrust catalogue record.

An earlier archive paper classes large text archives such as HathiTrust as having scale and no internal architecture, "collections, not systems", which a summarizer describes by what is in them without traversing how they work; the archive gives the native frame of digital libraries as collections, discovery, preservation and services evaluated as connected functions.
